options.text: The one-time movement of carbon from rocks into the air
The continuous movement of the same carbon atoms among the air, living things, oceans, and rocks
The process plants use to make oxygen from sunlight
The steady buildup of new carbon atoms made by living things

items.explanation: Carbon is never created or destroyed. The same carbon atoms keep moving among the air, living things, oceans, and rocks.

items.stem: How does carbon get out of the air and into a plant?

options.text: Plants absorb it through their roots from the soil
Animals breathe it directly into plants
Plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis
Rain washes it onto the plant's leaves

items.explanation: During photosynthesis, plant leaves absorb carbon dioxide from the air and use the carbon to build food.

items.stem: During photosynthesis, what does a plant do with carbon?

options.text: It removes carbon dioxide from the air and uses it to make food
It releases carbon dioxide into the air
It turns carbon straight into coal
It breaks down dead organisms

items.explanation: Photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide out of the air. This is the main way carbon enters the living world.

items.stem: When an animal eats a plant, what happens to the carbon in that plant?

options.text: It is destroyed
It evaporates into the air right away
It turns into sunlight
Some of it becomes part of the animal's body

items.explanation: Carbon passes along the food web. When an animal eats a plant, some of the carbon becomes part of the animal's body.

items.stem: Which process returns carbon to the air as living things release energy from their food?

options.text: Photosynthesis
Cellular respiration
Combustion of fossil fuels
Dissolving into the ocean

items.explanation: Cellular respiration releases energy from food and gives off carbon dioxide, returning carbon to the air.

items.stem: When plants and animals die, what usually happens to most of the carbon in their bodies?

options.text: Decomposers break them down and the carbon returns to the air and soil
It instantly turns into coal
It is launched into space
It stays locked inside the body forever

items.explanation: Decomposition breaks down dead organisms and returns most of their carbon to the air and soil.

items.stem: How did fossil fuels like coal form?

options.text: From volcanic ash that cooled over a few years
From ocean water evaporating and leaving carbon behind
From organisms that were buried and not fully decomposed over millions of years
From carbon dioxide freezing solid underground

items.explanation: Fossil fuels formed from plants and other organisms that were buried and not fully decomposed over millions of years.

items.stem: Which of these releases carbon stored underground back into the air quickly?

options.text: Photosynthesis in a forest
Carbon slowly dissolving in the deep ocean
Water soaking into the soil
Humans digging up and burning fossil fuels

items.explanation: Burning fossil fuels (combustion) releases stored carbon quickly. Volcanic eruptions do this too, but rarely.

items.stem: Besides the rocks and fuels underground, where is most of Earth's carbon stored?

options.text: In the clouds
Dissolved in the oceans
In the bodies of land animals
In bolts of lightning

items.explanation: The oceans are Earth's largest carbon store after the geosphere. Carbon dioxide dissolves into the water from the air.

items.stem: Why can scientists say the same carbon atoms are used over and over?

options.text: New carbon is constantly made by the Sun
Carbon leaves Earth and is replaced from space
Carbon is not created or destroyed; it just keeps moving among the air, living things, oceans, and rocks
Plants create brand new carbon during photosynthesis

items.explanation: Carbon is not created or destroyed. The same atoms cycle endlessly among the air, living things, oceans, and rocks.
